paper_context.research_question: Can automatically learned feature representations from readers' eye-movement (gaze) data, combined with textual embeddings via convolutional neural networks, improve sentiment polarity and sarcasm classification compared to (a) CNNs using text only and (b) existing systems that use handcrafted gaze and textual features?
contribution_style: comparative experiments on public gaze-enriched datasets
main_claims: A multimodal CNN that jointly learns features from text embeddings and eye-movement (fixation and saccade) channels yields better classification performance for sentiment polarity and sarcasm detection than (i) CNNs using text alone and (ii) existing systems based on handcrafted text+gaze features, on at least one published dataset.
Incorporating gaze data into CNNs consistently improves performance over text-only CNN variants (though gains vary across datasets and tasks).

Automatically learned gaze features capture linguistic subtleties (e.g., surprisal, semantic/pragmatic incongruity) that handcrafted features may miss, as evidenced by feature visualization and error analyses.

Model and dataset-specific factors (embedding dimension, static vs non-static channels, fixation vs saccade channels, dataset size/variance) influence whether the multimodal CNN outperforms traditional handcrafted-feature systems.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Classification performance metrics (precision/recall/F1) on sentiment and sarcasm datasets, comparing text-only CNN, gaze-only CNN, multimodal CNN, and prior handcrafted-feature baselines
Statistical significance testing of performance differences (e.g., McNemar test reported for some comparisons)

Ablation analyses across model variants: text channel types (static/non-static/multichannel), gaze channel types (fixation/saccade/multichannel), and hyperparameter settings (embedding dimension, filter sizes)
Robustness across datasets (differences in results between Dataset 1 and Dataset 2) and analysis of overfitting/regularization (training/validation behavior)
Qualitative analysis of learned feature representations and example-level error analysis illustrating when gaze helps
Scalability and sensitivity to ordering/representation of gaze scanpaths (noted constraint that P rows order is fixed)

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Eye-movement signals (fixation durations and saccade positions) recorded from multiple readers contain task-relevant information that can be learned by CNNs and generalized across examples to aid sentiment and sarcasm classification.
supporting_evidence: Section 2: citations and discussion linking surprisal and cognitive load to fixation/saccade patterns; Mishra et al. (2016b) observations.
Empirical tables (Tables 1 and 2) showing improved metrics when gaze channels are added.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If gaze signals are noisy, inconsistent across readers, or weakly correlated with labels, models may learn spurious patterns or overfit, reducing replicability and real-world utility.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Min-max normalization of fixation durations across participants sufficiently reduces subjectivity and makes fixation-duration channels comparable between readers.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2: "normalized durations of fixations... scaled across participants using min-max normalization to reduce subjectivity."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If min-max normalization fails to account for inter-participant differences or outliers, signals may be distorted or biased, degrading model performance or producing misleading features.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Keeping participant rows in a fixed order in the P×G gaze matrix does not introduce systematic artifacts that affect learned filters' validity.
supporting_evidence: Authors explicitly state they keep the order constant due to scalability concerns.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the model relies on arbitrary row-order artifacts, performance will degrade when participant ordering changes or when applied to different reader sets; generalization across readers may be compromised.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Pre-trained word2vec embeddings (dimension 50) initialized and optionally fine-tuned (non-static channel) are appropriate for these relatively small gaze-enriched datasets and help reduce overfitting compared to random or larger embeddings.
supporting_evidence: Section 5: authors report using pre-trained word2vec embeddings and that best results were obtained with embedding dimension 50; random initialization gave worse results.
Section 7: experiments varying embedding dimensions [50-300] reported best results at 50.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If small-dimension embeddings underfit or the pretrained vectors mismatch the domain, model performance could be suboptimal or brittle; conversely, small dimensions could mask model weaknesses.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: 2D convolutions across participants and sequence positions (J×J filters) are an appropriate inductive bias to capture shared gaze patterns relevant to classification.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2 explains 2D convolutions over P×G matrices and pooling; authors draw analogy to image filters capturing local spatial patterns.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If gaze patterns are not locally structured across adjacent participants/time windows or are highly participant-specific, 2D conv filters may miss relevant dependencies and limit performance gains.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The two gaze-derived channels (normalized fixation durations and fixation positions/word ids) sufficiently encode the informative aspects of scanpaths for sentiment and sarcasm classification.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.2 defines and uses these two channels as representing fixation and saccade information in experiments.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Other gaze signals (e.g., pupil size, fixation counts per word, inter-fixation intervals) might contain complementary information; excluding them may limit achievable performance or miss important behavior.

supporting_evidence: Section 5: "We follow the same 10-fold train-test configuration as these existing works for consistency."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If preprocessing, fold construction, or evaluation details differ, apparent performance differences may reflect protocol mismatches rather than model superiority.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Reported performance improvements are not primarily due to overfitting or chance given dataset sizes and model capacity.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that automatically learned representations from readers' gaze (fixations and saccades), processed via a 2D-CNN over participant×sequence matrices and merged with a standard 1D text-CNN, provide task-relevant features that improve sentiment polarity and sarcasm classification beyond text-only CNNs and prior handcrafted text+gaze systems. The empirical support rests on two published gaze-enriched datasets: Dataset1 (n=994, 7 readers) and Dataset2 (n=843, 5 readers). Reported results show statistically significant gains on Dataset1 (notably a 3.8% F improvement over the best prior text+gaze system; ≈5% improvement vs text-only CNNs) and smaller, dataset-dependent gains on Dataset2 (up to 2.9% vs text-only CNNs; CNNs do not beat handcrafted systems there). For sarcasm detection on Dataset1, CNNs provide large gains over traditional text-only baselines but adding gaze yields only a small, statistically insignificant improvement (~1.36%). The paper also presents qualitative visualizations of merged hidden-layer activations and interprets them as evidence that learned gaze features capture surprisal/semantic incongruity. Key architectural choices and operational assumptions (P×G representation, fixed participant row ordering, min-max normalization of fixation durations, embedding dimensionality=50, J×J 2D filters) are stated; several robustness and reporting limitations are acknowledged or remain untested (ordering sensitivity, per-fold variance, full significance testing across comparisons, systematic ablations). Overall, the chain of reasoning is plausible and partially supported by data, but some inferential steps (linking learned features to specific linguistic constructs and asserting consistency of gains) rest on limited experiments and selective statistical reporting.
logical_argument_graph: Premise P1: Eye-movements (fixations/saccades) correlate with linguistic subtleties (surprisal, cognitive load) — supported by prior psycholinguistics (Section 2).
Premise P2: Existing cognitive-NLP systems use handcrafted gaze features which may miss complex patterns (Introduction, related work).
Inference I1: CNNs can learn useful filters from structured inputs (analogy to images) and thus can replace manual feature engineering for gaze data (Sections 3–4).

Design D1: Represent gaze as P×G matrices with two channels (fixation durations, fixation positions/word ids) and apply 2D convolutions; represent text with 1D CNN (static/non-static/multichannel) and merge (Section 4).
Operational assumption A1: Min-max normalization and fixed participant ordering produce stable inputs for learning (Section 4.2; assumptions list).
Experiment E1: Train variants on two gaze-enriched datasets under 10-fold splits, compare text-only CNNs, gaze-only CNNs, combined CNNs, and prior handcrafted-feature baselines (Section 5).

Observation O1: On Dataset1, combined CNN variants outperform prior handcrafted text+gaze baselines (max F +3.8%, McNemar p<0.05) and outperform text-only CNNs (≈+5% F, p<0.05) (Section 6.1; Table 1).

Observation O2: On Dataset2, combined CNNs improve over text-only CNNs (up to +2.9% F) but do not surpass handcrafted-feature systems; training dynamics suggest overfitting (training accuracy →100%, validation ≈50%) (Section 6.1).
Observation O3: For sarcasm on Dataset1, CNNs greatly outperform classic baselines, but gaze addition yields only a minor (1.36%) and statistically insignificant improvement (Section 6.2; Table 2).

Inference I2: Learned gaze features help capture linguistic subtleties in at least some settings, supported by visualization of merge-layer activations showing more distinctive patterns for sarcastic vs non-sarcastic examples when gaze is included (Section 7; Figure 4).

Conclusion C: A multimodal CNN that learns gaze+text representations can provide meaningful improvements over text-only CNNs and can outperform handcrafted text+gaze systems in some dataset/model settings, though gains are dataset- and configuration-dependent and contingent on representation/training choices.

concerns.title: No assessment of participant-row ordering sensitivity

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run robustness checks: (a) train/evaluate with multiple random row orderings, (b) implement simple permutation-invariant aggregations (mean, max over participants) or attention across participants and compare, (c) report leave-one-reader-out performance to gauge reader-generalization.

transparency_notes: Authors report following the same 10-fold train-test splits as prior works, which improves comparability, but the manuscript should publish exact fold assignments and random seeds to enable reproducible replication.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The relative absence of prior deep-learning approaches for gaze-data feature learning is a sign of novelty, but novelty alone does not validate effectiveness; empirical robustness checks and ablations are needed to separate true signal exploitation from dataset-specific artifacts.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If gaze patterns generalize across diverse readers and texts (low inter-reader idiosyncrasy) and scanning behaviors correlate strongly with linguistic surprisal/pragmatic incongruity, the 2D CNN over P×G will learn transferable filters that improve classification.

If fixed ordering artifacts are minimal (or models are trained with randomized row-orders or permutation-invariant pooling), and improvements persist across permutations and leave-one-reader-out tests, the approach scales to unseen readers.

If systematic correlations between learned gaze-feature dimensions and independent linguistic metrics (e.g., surprisal, ambiguity) are demonstrated, the interpretive claim that learned features capture linguistic subtleties would be substantiated.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a multimodal CNN that jointly learns representations from text embeddings (1D convolutions) and readers' eye-movement data (2D convolutions over a P×G matrix where rows are participants and columns are scanpath positions). Experiments on two publicly available gaze-enriched datasets (Dataset1: 994 snippets with 7 readers; Dataset2: 843 snippets with 5 readers) compare many CNN variants (static/non-static/multichannel text; fixation/saccade/multichannel gaze) against text-only CNNs and prior handcrafted text+gaze systems (Mishra et al.). Reported results show statistically significant improvements (McNemar) for several multimodal variants on Dataset1 (largest +3.8 F over prior best; ≈+5 F over text-only CNNs). Dataset2 shows smaller gains; CNNs do not beat handcrafted systems there and show signs of overfitting. The gaze component requires fixed participant ordering and uses min-max normalization of fixation durations. Qualitative visualization of merge-layer activations is used to argue that learned gaze features capture linguistic subtleties. The paper's empirical claim depends critically on (i) the informativeness and cross-reader consistency of gaze signals, (ii) fairness and matching of train/test splits and preprocessing relative to baselines, (iii) robustness to participant-row ordering and normalization choices, and (iv) the stability of gains under hyperparameter choices and statistical variance across folds.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes a multimodal CNN that jointly learns features from text embeddings and readers' eye-movement data (encoded as P×G matrices with fixation and saccade channels). The authors argue that (1) automatically learned gaze features improve sentiment and sarcasm classification over text-only CNNs and prior handcrafted text+gaze systems, (2) learned gaze features capture linguistic subtleties such as surprisal and pragmatic incongruity, and (3) gains depend on model and dataset factors (embedding size, channel types, dataset size/variance). Empirically, the strongest evidence is on Dataset1 (sentiment and sarcasm), with statistically significant F-score improvements over prior handcrafted baselines and over text-only CNNs. Dataset2 shows smaller gains and signs of overfitting. Methodologically, the novelty is the 2D convolutional treatment of many readers' scanpaths and the merge of those learned features with standard 1D text CNN features. However, several design choices (fixed participant-row ordering, limited hyperparameter search, selective statistical testing, anecdotal feature visualizations) leave open alternative explanations for the reported improvements (e.g., overfitting, data artifacts, ordering effects). The paper reads as an incremental but meaningful extension of prior cognitive-NLP work: it replaces manual gaze feature engineering with learned representations and explores architectural variants; empirical support is promising but dataset-limited and would benefit from robustness checks and more transparent statistical reporting.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a multimodal CNN that jointly learns features from textual embeddings (static/non-static/multi-channel 1D convolutions) and eye-movement (fixation duration and saccade position channels represented as P×G matrices processed with 2D convolutions). The core empirical claim is that learned gaze features improve sentiment and sarcasm classification relative to text-only CNNs and prior handcrafted text+gaze systems, with strongest evidence on Dataset1 (up to +3.8% F; McNemar p<0.05). The authors argue that learned gaze features capture linguistic subtleties (surprisal, semantic/pragmatic incongruity) and show qualitative merge-layer visualizations suggesting improved separability for sarcastic cases when gaze is included. They also report that gains depend on modeling and data choices (embedding dimensionality, fixation vs saccade channels, static vs non-static embeddings), and acknowledge limitations including fixed participant-row ordering and limited hyperparameter tuning. The manuscript's reasoning chain: (1) human gaze reflects cognitive processing linked to linguistic subtlety; (2) CNNs can learn filters from gaze matrices analogous to image filters; (3) combining learned gaze features with text embeddings yields better representations for classification; (4) empirical tests on two public gaze-enriched datasets show improvements, but dataset- and model-specific factors modulate effect sizes. Several methodological gaps (selective significance reporting, ordering sensitivity, limited ablation statistics, and anecdotal visualization) leave open alternative explanations (overfitting, dataset idiosyncrasy, ordering artifacts). Nonetheless, the conceptual framing—automatically learning cognitive features from gaze via 2D convolutions over reader×time matrices—is not a close analog to mainstream multimodal NLP pipelines and should be treated as a potentially disruptive idea meriting robustness checks rather than penalization for divergence.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a multimodal CNN that jointly learns representations from text embeddings (1D convolutions; static/non-static/multi-channel variants) and readers' eye-movement data encoded as P×G matrices processed with 2D convolutions (fixation durations and fixation positions/saccades as channels). Empirically, on two published gaze-enriched datasets (Dataset1: n=994, 7 readers; Dataset2: n=843, 5 readers), the multimodal CNN variants show meaningful improvements over text-only CNNs and over previously reported handcrafted text+gaze systems on Dataset1 (largest reported +3.8 F over best prior text+gaze system; ≈+5 F over text-only CNNs; McNemar p<0.05 mentioned). Gains on Dataset2 are smaller and CNNs do not surpass handcrafted-feature systems there; Dataset2 also shows signs of overfitting. For sarcasm detection, text-only CNNs already achieve large gains over traditional baselines; adding gaze provides only small, statistically insignificant improvements. The authors present qualitative merge-layer visualizations and interpret higher activation intensity as learned sensitivity to linguistic subtleties (surprisal, incongruity). Key methodological choices include min-max normalization of fixation durations, fixed participant-row ordering in P×G matrices, limited hyperparameter search (embedding dim best at 50), and selective statistical reporting. Overall, the central empirical claim (learned gaze features can help classification) is supported for at least one dataset (Dataset1) but broader claims of consistency and linguistic interpretability are partially supported and rest on limited evidence and some untested assumptions.
logical_argument_graph: Premise: Human gaze patterns correlate with cognitive processing linked to linguistic subtleties (Section 2).
Design: Encode gaze scanpaths from multiple readers as a P×G matrix with two channels (fixation duration, fixation position) and apply 2D convolutions to learn features (Section 4.2).
Design: Use standard 1D text CNN (static/non-static/multi-channel embeddings) to learn textual features and merge with gaze-derived features at a fully connected merge layer (Sections 4.1, 4.2).
Empirical test: Evaluate many CNN variants and baselines on two public gaze-enriched datasets following the same 10-fold splits as prior work (Section 5).
Observation: On Dataset1 multimodal CNNs outperform text-only CNNs and prior handcrafted text+gaze systems; improvements reported as statistically significant (Section 6.1; Table 1).
Observation: On Dataset2 improvements are smaller; CNNs do not beat handcrafted systems and training shows overfitting (Section 6.1).
Interpretation: Visualized merge-layer activations suggest learned gaze features capture surprisal/incongruity for some examples (Section 7; Figure 4).
Conclusion: Learned gaze representations can improve sentiment and sarcasm classification, but gains are dataset- and model-dependent and require further robustness checks (Sections 6–7).

strengths.title: Empirical gains demonstrated on a public dataset
strengths.description: On Dataset1, multimodal CNN variants report statistically significant improvements over both text-only CNNs and prior handcrafted text+gaze systems, supporting the core hypothesis that learned gaze features can help classification.
evidence: Table 1: NONSTATICTEXT + MULTICHANNELGAZE F = 77.3 vs prior Text+Gaze (Best) F = 73.5; Section 6.1 notes McNemar p < 0.05.
Reported ≈5% improvement of multimodal CNNs over text-only CNN variants on Dataset1.

strengths.title: Thoughtful discussion of limitations and model variants
strengths.description: The authors acknowledge key limitations (participant ordering, dataset overfitting, limited hyperparameter tuning) and discuss the influence of model choices (embedding dimension, channel types) on results.
evidence: Sections 4.2 and 7 explicitly discuss ordering limitation and overfitting on Dataset2; Section 5 describes hyperparameter choices and trial-and-error tuning.
Section 7 contains analyses of embedding dimension, static vs non-static channels, and fixation vs saccade effects.

concerns.title: Selective and incomplete statistical reporting
concerns.description: Statistical significance is reported selectively (McNemar p < 0.05 reported for some Dataset1 comparisons) but the manuscript lacks full details: which paired comparisons were tested, per-fold contingency counts used by McNemar, p-values for all key comparisons, and confidence intervals or standard errors for reported metrics.
evidence: Section 6.1 references McNemar p < 0.05 for Dataset1 but does not give exact contingency tables, per-fold results, or p-values for other comparisons.
Shared analysis and prior-stage digests note absence of per-fold variance or confidence intervals.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide per-fold precision/recall/F1 for all 10 folds for each model variant; include paired statistical tests (McNemar or bootstrap-based) with full contingency tables or test statistics and p-values for every principal pairwise comparison (multimodal vs text-only; multimodal vs prior best). Also include 95% confidence intervals or standard deviations for reported metrics.

concerns.title: Participant-row ordering dependency untested
concerns.description: The gaze component is not permutation-invariant: the P rows (participants) are kept in a fixed order during training/testing. No experiments assess sensitivity to this arbitrary ordering, risking that the model may exploit ordering artifacts rather than true cross-reader patterns.
evidence: Section 4.2 explicitly states the P rows cannot be shuffled and that training/testing keep a constant order.
Shared analysis and prior-stage digests highlight lack of experiments testing ordering sensitivity.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run experiments that (a) randomly permute participant row order across folds and report performance variability, (b) train with multiple random orderings and average results, (c) implement permutation-invariant alternatives (e.g., per-participant encoding then pooling or attention over readers) or test leave-one-reader-out performance to assess generalization.

concerns.title: Anecdotal feature-visualization without systematic validation
concerns.description: Claims that learned gaze features capture surprisal and semantic/pragmatic incongruity rely on a small number of visualized examples and qualitative interpretation; no quantitative correlation with linguistic measures (e.g., surprisal scores) or systematic clustering/feature attribution is provided.
evidence: Section 7 and Figure 4 show visualizations for four examples and interpret increased activation intensity as capturing sarcasm-related features.
Shared analysis notes visualization evidence is anecdotal and not tied quantitatively to linguistic variables.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantitatively evaluate learned gaze-derived features by correlating feature activations with linguistic measures (word/sentence surprisal from a language model, syntactic complexity, presence of incongruity markers). Provide aggregate analyses (e.g., feature importance, clustering, or probing classifiers) over many examples rather than a few anecdotes.

concerns.title: Limited hyperparameter exploration and potential overfitting
concerns.description: Hyperparameter tuning is described as trial-and-error with a small reported sweep for embedding dimension; other settings (number of filters, filter sizes, dropout, optimizer parameters) were fixed heuristically. Dataset2 shows overfitting (100% train acc within 25 epochs) suggesting capacity/settings need systematic tuning or stronger regularization.
evidence: Section 5 states hyperparameters are fixed by trial and error; Section 7 reports embedding dim experiments but limited exploration elsewhere.
Section 6.1 notes Dataset2 training accuracy reaches 100% with validation ~50%.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide systematic hyperparameter searches (grid or random) or at least sensitivity analyses for key parameters (embedding dim, filter widths/number, dropout rates, learning rate, batch size, early stopping). For Dataset2, try stronger regularization, early stopping, reduced capacity, or data augmentation and report results.

concerns.title: Insufficient preprocessing and missing-data detail for gaze signals
concerns.description: The paper gives only a brief description of min-max normalization of fixation durations; details about handling missing fixations, varying scanpath lengths (padding/truncation), outliers, and alignment to tokenization are not fully specified, which hampers reproducibility and may affect results.
evidence: Section 4.2 mentions min-max normalization and padding of text sequences but lacks detail on missing gaze entries or how fixation positions map to word tokens.
Shared analysis notes preprocessing details (normalization parameters, missing-data handling) are not fully specified.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Document preprocessing steps: how scanpaths with fewer/more fixations are padded/truncated, rules for aligning fixation positions to word ids, treatment of blinks/missing data, and min-max scaling ranges and whether scaling is per-participant or global. Include a short appendix with code snippets or pseudocode for reproducibility.

comparable_works.relevance: Direct prior work using handcrafted gaze+text features for sentiment and sarcasm on same datasets; main comparison baseline.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This paper replaces handcrafted gaze features with learned gaze representations via 2D convolutions and reports better results on Dataset1 but not on Dataset2.
comparable_works.source_trace: Sections 1, 5, 6; Table 1 and 2 reference Mishra et al. (2016b,c) as baselines

comparable_works.relevance: Text-CNN architecture used as the textual baseline (text-only CNN variants replicate Kim's approach).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Authors use static/non-static/multi-channel variants of Kim's CNN for the text component and show gains when adding the gaze component.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 4.1 and multiple comparisons in Tables 1 and 2

comparable_works.citation_label: Related cognitive-NLP works (Klerke et al., Barrett & Søgaard, Riloff et al.)
comparable_works.relevance: Context for use of behavioral signals / gaze in NLP tasks and prior feature engineering approaches for sarcasm.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Prior works use gaze features for other tasks or handcrafted features; this paper's learned 2D conv approach lacks close analogs in mainstream multimodal pipelines but is incrementally building on cognitive-NLP literature.

uncertainty_flags: Selective statistical testing and missing per-fold metrics reduce confidence in robustness of reported improvements.
Fixed participant-row ordering is an untested design constraint that could introduce artifacts.
Feature-visualization evidence is anecdotal and not quantitatively validated.
Hyperparameter tuning is limited and results may be sensitive to settings.
Dataset sizes are modest and Dataset2 shows overfitting, limiting generalizability.
alternative_interpretations: Performance gains on Dataset1 could partly stem from dataset-specific artifacts or favorable splits (e.g., participant ordering or correlation between reader patterns and labels) rather than generalizable gaze-derived signal.

High model capacity combined with limited dataset size could allow the multimodal CNN to memorize training idiosyncrasies (especially with fixed reader ordering), inflating test performance on some splits.

Merge-layer activation differences might reflect encoding of reader idiosyncrasies or formatting cues rather than linguistic surprisal or incongruity; without correlation analysis this remains ambiguous.

Small embedding dimensions (K=50) helping performance may indicate that the network benefits from reduced capacity more than from superior semantic representation; different regularization strategies could change rankings.
transparency_notes: Require per-fold (10 folds) metrics and full paired-test details to allow reproduction and fair comparison with prior work.
Provide code or pseudocode for gaze preprocessing (min-max scaling procedure, padding/truncation, mapping of fixation positions to tokens) to ensure reproducibility.
Report exact implementation details of statistical tests (McNemar contingency formation: aggregated across folds vs single combined test), random seeds, and number of random restarts.
Disclose participant ordering used in experiments and include scripts to reproduce ordering or permute it for robustness checks.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The 2D convolutional treatment of multiple readers' scanpaths encoded as a P×G matrix is not a close analog of common multimodal approaches; this divergence is a plausible innovation signal but does not by itself validate the empirical claims—robustness checks are required to separate novelty from dataset artifacts.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If gaze signals are reliably correlated with linguistic surprisal or incongruity across many readers and texts, learned 2D filters can capture consistent patterns and generalize.
If participant ordering is rendered irrelevant by permutation-invariant aggregation (e.g., pooling/attention over readers), the approach could scale and avoid ordering artifacts.
If systematic hyperparameter tuning and stronger regularization reduce overfitting on small datasets, the multimodal model's gains should persist.
If learned gaze features quantitatively correlate with external linguistic measures (surprisal, syntactic complexity), the interpretability claims would be strengthened.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Replacing handcrafted gaze features with learned representations and applying 2D convolutions to participant×time gaze matrices is a principled and meaningful extension of prior cognitive-NLP work; however, it builds on established CNN fusion practices and differs mainly in the particular encoding of gaze.
evidence: Sections 4.1–4.2: architecture combining 1D text-CNN and 2D gaze-CNN; Related work cites Mishra et al. employing handcrafted gaze features.
uncertainty_flags: The paper lacks comparisons to alternative permutation-invariant encodings for multi-reader gaze, so claimed architectural novelty may be narrower than presented.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Treating multi-reader scanpaths as 2D images for convolutional feature learning is conceptually distinct from prior approaches and could open a new modality-encoding direction, but current evidence is dataset-limited and some core methodological gaps (ordering sensitivity, statistical rigor) must be addressed to support disruptive claims.
evidence: Explicit discussion in Section 4.2 about 2D convs over P×G matrices and the lack of similar mainstream analogs in Related Work.
Empirical improvement on at least one public dataset (Dataset1).
uncertainty_flags: Robustness to ordering and generalization to new datasets/readers is not demonstrated; innovation may not translate to consistent practical advantage without further validation.

confidence_interval.rationale: Based on the manuscript excerpts and shared analyses, there is moderate confidence that the core claim (learned gaze features can help classification) holds for Dataset1 but lower confidence for broad generalization across datasets and tasks due to selective statistical reporting, untested ordering sensitivity, limited hyperparameter tuning, and anecdotal feature analyses.

consensus_findings: The paper proposes a clear, implementable multimodal CNN that merges a 1D text-branch with a 2D gaze-branch (P×G matrices with fixation and saccade channels); this architectural idea is coherently presented and suitably novel within the cognitive-NLP literature.

Empirical results show measurable improvements on at least one public dataset (Dataset1): several multimodal CNN variants outperform both text-only CNN baselines and previously reported handcrafted text+gaze systems; the manuscript reports a maximum F improvement of ≈3.8% over the best prior text+gaze system and larger gains versus text-only CNNs on Dataset1.

Results are dataset-dependent: Dataset2 yields smaller or inconsistent gains and shows training dynamics indicative of overfitting (training accuracy reaches 100% quickly while validation remains low), so claimed benefits do not uniformly generalize across the two evaluated datasets.

The manuscript documents many reasonable engineering choices (embedding initialization, channel variants, filter sizes) and explores multiple model configurations, which aids interpretability of which variants perform better in the reported setting.
disagreements: Magnitude and generality of the benefit from gaze: reviewers agree there is a benefit on Dataset1 but differ in how strong and general that signal is—some view Dataset1 gains as credible evidence of usefulness, others emphasize that Dataset2 and sarcasm results attenuate the generality claim.

Interpretability of learned gaze features: some reviewers find the visualization evidence suggestive and plausibly supportive of the claim that learned gaze features capture linguistic subtleties; others treat these visualizations as anecdotal and insufficient without quantitative validation.

Novelty framing: reviewers differ in tone between 'incremental engineering advance' (learned vs handcrafted gaze features) and 'potentially disruptive conceptual idea' (treating multi-reader scanpaths as 2D arrays for convolution). All agree novelty exists, but they disagree on how far that novelty extends absent robustness checks.
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical reporting and variability: per-fold metrics, standard deviations/confidence intervals, exact contingency tables for McNemar tests, and whether multiple-comparison corrections were applied are missing or reported selectively.

Participant-row ordering (P dimension) dependency: the gaze branch requires a fixed ordering of participant rows; no experiments test sensitivity to row permutations, nor are permutation-invariant alternatives (pooling/attention/set-based encodings) evaluated.

Overfitting and hyperparameter sensitivity: Dataset2 shows clear signs of overfitting; hyperparameter selection is described as heuristic with limited sweeps, raising uncertainty about whether reported gains are robust to reasonable hyperparameter changes.

Preprocessing and data-handling details for gaze signals: min-max normalization specifics, outlier treatment, handling of missing gaze data, and padding/truncation of scanpaths are under-specified, impacting reproducibility and possibly results.

Interpretive claims from visualization: anecdotal merge-layer visualizations are not systematically linked to independent linguistic measures (e.g., surprisal), so the claim that learned gaze features capture specific linguistic subtleties remains under-evidenced.
model_diversity_effects: Embedding dimensionality and channel setup influence results: reported best-performing embedding dimension was small (K=50) and multi-channel/static-vs-nonstatic text channels change rankings; reviewers flagged that such choices could reflect reduced capacity/overfitting control rather than superior semantic encoding.

Gaze-channel composition matters: variants using saccade channels were reported to help semantic incongruity in the authors' analysis, while fixation-only channels showed higher variance across runs/datasets—this suggests the relative utility of fixation vs saccade inputs is task- and dataset-dependent.

Model capacity and additional parameters from adding gaze channels may contribute to gains: several reviewers noted that increases in model capacity (extra branch, extra filters) could be partly responsible for improved performance unless controlled for (e.g., capacity-matched baselines).

Ordering and reader-specific effects can interact with model choice: because the gaze representation fixes participant order, model variants may implicitly exploit positional encodings tied to particular readers or cohorts; cross-reader generalization (leave-one-reader-out) and permutation-invariant variants could alter which model variants appear best.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Place the authors' manuscript into a revision cycle requesting focused empirical and reporting improvements before further editorial advancement. Specifically, request that authors (a) provide full per-fold results (10 folds) and report mean ± standard deviation or bootstrap confidence intervals for all main metrics; (b) disclose exact statistical test implementations and present contingency tables and exact p-values for all claimed pairwise significance tests, with multiple-comparison controls where appropriate; (c) run robustness experiments assessing sensitivity to participant-row ordering (random permutations, several random orderings during training/testing) and report results; (d) evaluate permutation-invariant or set-based alternatives (simple pooling across readers, attention over reader dimension, or leave-one-reader-out) to demonstrate that gains are not ordering artifacts; (e) carry out systematic hyperparameter sensitivity analyses (embedding dims, filter widths/counts, dropout, l2, learning rate) and present learning curves showing training vs validation dynamics for representative variants to address overfitting concerns; (f) provide quantitative analyses linking learned gaze-feature activations to independent linguistic measures (e.g., surprisal from a language model, syntactic complexity) or present probing/clustering statistics to substantiate interpretability claims; and (g) release code, exact data splits/fold indices, normalization scripts, and random seeds to enable reproducibility checks. Emphasize that the editor remains the central decision-maker: these items are required for the editor to judge robustness and generalizability, not for reviewers to re-decide acceptance in place of the editor.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript, perform and report the following concrete steps: (1) Reproducibility/reporting: publish the exact 10-fold split files, random seeds, preprocessing and normalization code (min-max formulas, outlier handling, padding/truncation rules), and the model training scripts. Include per-fold metrics and mean ± stddev or 95% CIs for precision/recall/F1 for each model variant. (2) Statistical rigor: For every principal pairwise comparison (multimodal vs text-only; multimodal vs prior best), provide paired test details (McNemar or bootstrap), contingency tables or bootstrap distributions, exact p-values, and note any multiple-comparison adjustments. (3) Ordering robustness: Run experiments with multiple random permutations of participant rows and report variance; implement at least one permutation-invariant alternative (e.g., per-participant encoding + max/mean pooling or attention over participants) and compare. (4) Reader generalization: Run leave-one-reader-out or reader-holdout tests to evaluate whether the model exploits reader-specific idiosyncrasies. (5) Ablations & capacity controls: Provide targeted ablations isolating fixation vs saccade channels, single- vs multi-channel gaze, and a capacity-matched baseline that adds an auxiliary random channel of comparable parameter count to rule out gains from increased capacity alone. (6) Hyperparameter and regularization sweeps: Systematically sweep key hyperparameters, report learning curves and early-stopping behavior, and show results with stronger regularization on Dataset2 to demonstrate whether overfitting can be mitigated while preserving gains. (7) Interpretability: Quantitatively correlate learned gaze-feature activations (or selected filter responses) with independent linguistic metrics (surprisal, dependency distance, syntactic depth) across the dataset and report aggregate statistics, not just examples. (8) Documentation: Add an appendix or supplement with all experimental settings, full result tables, and guidance to reproduce the reported experiments.
transparency_report: Missing per-fold (10-fold) metric distributions (means and variances) for each reported model variant and dataset.
Incomplete statistical test details: exact contingency tables or test statistics, p-values, whether tests are one- or two-sided, and whether multiple-comparison corrections were applied.

Under-specified preprocessing of gaze data: exact min-max normalization formula (per-participant vs global), outlier handling, mapping of fixation positions to word tokens, and padding/truncation procedure for variable-length scanpaths.
No reported experiments testing sensitivity to participant-row ordering or permutation-invariant alternatives; ordering used in experiments was not published.
Limited hyperparameter-search logs and lack of learning curves showing training/validation trajectories for representative variants, especially for Dataset2 where overfitting was observed.
Code and split files not included in the current report excerpts (authors should release code, data-split files, and random seeds).
epistemic_limits: Based on the submitted material and specialist reviews, we cannot conclusively determine: (a) that learned gaze representations will reliably improve sentiment/sarcasm classification across domains and reader cohorts beyond the evaluated datasets, because only two modest-sized datasets were used and one exhibits overfitting; (b) whether the reported gains stem from informative gaze-derived cognitive signals (e.g., surprisal) rather than from dataset-specific artifacts, reader-specific idiosyncrasies, or increases in model capacity, because permutation and leave-one-reader-out tests and capacity-matched controls are absent; (c) the statistical robustness of claimed improvements across random splits and initializations, because per-fold variance and full test-statistics are not provided; and (d) the claimed interpretability mapping between learned gaze features and specific linguistic constructs, because visualization evidence is anecdotal and not supported by systematic quantitative correlations. These limits can be reduced by the robustness and transparency experiments requested above; until they are addressed, the generality and mechanistic interpretation of the results remain provisional.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript introduces a multimodal CNN that jointly learns representations from text (1D CNN with static/non-static/multi-channel embeddings) and readers' eye-movement data encoded as P×G matrices (2D convolutions over fixation durations and fixation positions/saccades). Empirical evaluation on two public gaze-enriched datasets shows clear improvements on Dataset1 (several multimodal variants outperform text-only CNNs and reported handcrafted text+gaze baselines; a maximum reported F improvement ≈3.8% with a McNemar test claim) and smaller/inconsistent gains on Dataset2 (signs of overfitting). Visualizations of merged hidden-layer activations are presented to argue that learned gaze features capture linguistic subtleties. Reviewers find the architectural idea coherent and potentially novel in cognitive-NLP, but raise reproducibility and robustness issues (selective statistical reporting, untested sensitivity to participant-row ordering in P×G matrices, limited hyperparameter sweeps, under-specified preprocessing, and anecdotal feature visualizations).
strengths: Clear, implementable multimodal architecture: 1D text-CNN merged with a 2D gaze-CNN over P×G input (Sections 4.1–4.2; Figure 3).

Empirical evaluation on public gaze-enriched datasets with multiple model variants (text-only, gaze-only, combined) and comparisons to prior handcrafted text+gaze baselines (Tables 1–2; comparison to Mishra et al.).

Authors acknowledge limitations (fixed participant ordering, overfitting on Dataset2) and explore multiple architectural ablations (static/non-static embeddings; fixation vs saccade channels), which clarifies where gains arise.
limitations: Selective and underspecified statistical reporting: McNemar test is mentioned for some Dataset1 comparisons but exact contingency tables, per-fold outcomes, per-fold means ± stddev or confidence intervals, and multiple-comparison handling are not provided—this impedes assessment of robustness of claimed significance.

Participant-row ordering dependency: the gaze branch encodes P×G with a fixed participant-row order and no experiments assess sensitivity to permutations, permutation-invariant alternatives (pooling/attention), or leave-one-reader-out generalization; this leaves open the possibility that learned filters exploit arbitrary ordering artifacts or reader idiosyncrasies.

Hyperparameter tuning and overfitting concerns: hyperparameters are set by trial-and-error with limited sweeps; Dataset2 exhibits training accuracy reaching 100% with low validation, yet remedies (systematic regularization, capacity controls, learning curves) are not systematically reported.

Preprocessing and data-handling underspecified: exact min-max normalization procedure (per-participant vs global), outlier handling, mapping of fixation positions to word tokens, padding/truncation or imputation for variable-length scanpaths, and fold files/seeds are not fully detailed, reducing reproducibility.

Interpretability evidence is anecdotal: visualization of merge-layer activations (Figure 4) is limited to few examples and lacks quantitative correlation with independent linguistic measures (e.g., surprisal), so claims that learned gaze features capture specific linguistic subtleties remain provisional.
open_questions: Please provide per-fold (10-fold) precision/recall/F1 for all reported model variants and datasets, plus mean ± standard deviation or 95% confidence intervals; for which exact model pairs was McNemar applied and what are the contingency tables and exact p-values?

How sensitive are results to participant-row ordering? Run experiments with multiple random permutations of P rows and report variance; additionally, test at least one permutation-invariant alternative (per-participant encoding + pooling or attention) and leave-one-reader-out evaluations.

What exact preprocessing steps were used for gaze (min-max normalization details: per-participant or global scaling, clipping/outlier rules), how were variable-length scanpaths padded/truncated or imputed, and how were fixation positions aligned to token indices? Please provide code or pseudocode.

Provide systematic hyperparameter/regularization sensitivity analyses (embedding dimensions, filter sizes/counts, dropout, l2, learning rates) and learning curves for representative models—especially Dataset2 where training suggests overfitting. Do gains persist under stronger regularization or capacity-matched baselines?

Can the authors quantify the interpretability claim by correlating learned gaze-feature activations or filter responses with independent linguistic metrics (surprisal from a language model, dependency distance, syntactic complexity) across the datasets rather than only showing example visualizations?

Were comparisons to prior handcrafted baselines run on the identical splits and preprocessing as the current models (exact fold files and random seeds)? Please release split files and seeds to ensure fairness of comparisons.
consensus_snapshot: Architectural contribution is clear and meaningfully novel in this subfield: representing multi-reader scanpaths as P×G matrices and applying 2D convolutions is a coherent engineering approach (Sections 4.2; Figure 3).

Empirical gains are credible on Dataset1: multiple multimodal variants report higher F-scores than text-only CNNs and prior handcrafted text+gaze baselines (Table 1), with authors stating McNemar p < 0.05 for at least one comparison.
Results are dataset-dependent: Dataset2 shows smaller or no gains and clear signs of overfitting, so conclusions about consistent, general improvements across datasets/tasks are not established.
Key reproducibility and robustness elements (per-fold metrics, permutation tests, preprocessing code, hyperparameter sweeps) are missing and should be provided to substantiate generalization claims.
disagreement_snapshot: Some reviewers interpret Dataset1 improvements and reported McNemar test mention as reasonably strong evidence that learned gaze features can help classification in at least some settings; others stress that without per-fold statistics and ordering robustness tests the improvement could reflect artifacts (ordering, splits, reader idiosyncrasy) or additional model capacity rather than robust gaze signal.

Interpretability via visualization: a subset of reviewers find the visualizations suggestive and consistent with the theoretical motivation (surprisal related to fixations), while others treat these as anecdotal and request systematic quantitative validation before accepting the linguistic-subtlety claim.

Novelty framing: reviewers agree the approach is novel relative to prior handcrafted-gaze work (Mishra et al.), but differ on whether the contribution is an incremental engineering extension or a potentially disruptive modality-encoding idea—this hinges on whether robustness/transfer experiments succeed.
uncertainty_snapshot: Statistical robustness: uncertain because per-fold variance and full test-statistics are not reported; selective p-value reporting increases the chance of reporting instability.
Ordering and reader-generalization: unknown sensitivity to P-row order and reader composition; absence of permutation/leave-one-reader-out tests is a major uncertainty source.
Overfitting/generalizability: Dataset2 training dynamics indicate overfitting; it is uncertain whether reported gains generalize beyond current datasets or hyperparameter choices.

Interpretability mechanistic claim: unclear whether learned gaze features map reliably to linguistic constructs (surprisal/incongruity) because visualization evidence is limited and not quantitatively correlated to linguistic metrics.
source_trace: Architecture and P×G gaze encoding: manuscript Section 4.2 and Figure 3 (description of P×G matrix, two gaze channels, and 2D convolutions).
Empirical results and Dataset1 gains: manuscript Section 6.1 and Table 1 (NONSTATICTEXT + MULTICHANNELGAZE F = 77.3 vs prior Text+Gaze Best = 73.5; stated McNemar p < 0.05).
Dataset2 overfitting and variable gains: manuscript Section 6.1 (training accuracy reaches 100% within 25 epochs while validation remains ~50%).

Feature visualizations and interpretability claim: manuscript Section 7 and Figure 4 (merge-layer activations compared between MULTICHANNELTEXT and MULTICHANNELTEXT+MULTICHANNELGAZE for example sentences).
Related prior work (handcrafted gaze features): Mishra et al. (2016b, 2016c) cited throughout as baselines (Tables 1–2 and Related Work).
Text-CNN baseline architecture grounding: Kim (2014) used as canonical text-CNN template for text component (Section 4.1).
transparency_notes: The submission omits several reproducibility-critical artifacts: per-fold results (10 folds) and mean±std or confidence intervals for all reported metrics; exact McNemar contingency tables and p-values for each pairwise test; full preprocessing details and code for gaze normalization (min-max formula, per-participant vs global), padding/truncation/imputation of scanpaths and mapping to token indices; fold assignment files and random seeds; and logs/plots for hyperparameter searches and learning curves. Authors are encouraged to release code/scripts and split files in a supplement or repository.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request a targeted revision focused on robustness, reproducibility, and interpretability before further editorial consideration. Required items: (1) publish per-fold metrics (10 folds) and report mean ± stddev or 95% CI for precision/recall/F1 for each model and dataset; (2) disclose exact McNemar implementation and report contingency tables and exact p-values for all principal pairwise comparisons (multimodal vs text-only; multimodal vs prior best), and apply/describe any multiple-comparison adjustments; (3) run ordering-robustness experiments (multiple random permutations of participant rows during training/testing) and at least one permutation-invariant alternative (per-participant encoding + pooling or attention) plus leave-one-reader-out tests; (4) perform systematic hyperparameter and regularization sweeps and present learning curves (train vs validation) for representative variants, addressing Dataset2 overfitting; (5) add quantitative analyses correlating learned gaze-feature activations with independent linguistic measures (e.g., surprisal from a language model, syntactic complexity), beyond anecdotal visualizations; (6) release preprocessing/normalization scripts, fold indices, and random seeds to enable independent replication. Frame these as mandatory revision items to resolve main epistemic uncertainties, not as optional improvements.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidential claims and address reviewer concerns, provide the following: (A) Complete reporting: per-fold results for all reported variants, mean±std or bootstrap 95% CIs; exact McNemar contingency tables, p-values, and note corrections for multiple comparisons. (B) Reproducibility artifacts: release code or scripts that build P×G matrices, the normalization pipeline (explicit min-max formulas and whether scaling is per-participant or global), padding/truncation/imputation rules, token alignment, the 10-fold split files, and random seeds. (C) Ordering and generalization tests: run experiments with randomized participant-row permutations (multiple seeds) and report variance; implement a permutation-invariant baseline (e.g., per-participant encoding + mean/max pooling or attention) and perform leave-one-reader-out evaluation. (D) Ablations and capacity controls: isolate fixation vs saccade contributions, compare multi-channel gaze vs single-channel, and include a capacity-matched baseline that adds an auxiliary random channel (same parameter count) to rule out gains from extra capacity alone. (E) Hyperparameter sweeps and overfitting mitigation: systematically sweep embedding sizes, filter sizes/counts, dropout/l2, learning rates; provide learning curves and try stronger regularization or smaller-capacity variants for Dataset2 to show whether gains persist. (F) Interpretability analyses: compute correlations or predictive probes between learned gaze activations (or filter responses) and linguistic metrics (surprisal, dependency distance, presence of incongruity markers) on the full datasets and report aggregate statistics. (G) Documentation: add an appendix summarizing all experimental settings, seeds, and scripts to reproduce the main tables and visualizations.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The manuscript proposes a multimodal CNN that learns gaze-derived features from P×G scanpath matrices via 2D convolutions and merges them with 1D text-CNN features. Experiments on two public gaze-enriched datasets show meaningful improvements on Dataset1 (several multimodal variants outperform text-only CNNs and prior handcrafted text+gaze baselines; authors report a maximum ≈3.8% F improvement and a McNemar p < 0.05 claim) and smaller or inconsistent gains on Dataset2, which shows overfitting behavior. Visualizations of merge-layer activations are used to argue that learned gaze features reflect linguistic subtleties.

Strengths:
- Clear architectural formulation: P×G gaze encoding and 2D convolutional processing merged with text-CNN is a coherent and implementable idea (Figure 3). 
- Empirical evaluation on public gaze-enriched datasets with many model variants and direct comparison to prior handcrafted-feature baselines (Tables 1–2; Mishra et al.).
- Authors acknowledge limitations and explore variants (fixation vs saccade channels, static/non-static embeddings), aiding interpretability of where gains occur.

Limitations:
- Statistical reporting is incomplete: per-fold metrics, confidence intervals, contingency tables and exact p-values for McNemar are missing; selective significance reporting reduces confidence in robustness. 
- The gaze representation depends on a fixed participant-row order with no permutation-sensitivity experiments; thus performance may rely on arbitrary ordering or reader-specific artifacts. 
- Hyperparameter tuning is limited and Dataset2 shows overfitting; learning curves and regularization sweeps are not systematically reported. 
- Preprocessing of gaze (normalization specifics, padding/truncation, mapping to tokens, missing-data handling) is under-documented, hampering reproducibility. 
- Interpretability claims rest on a few visualization examples; quantitative correlation to linguistic measures is absent.

Open Questions:
1) Provide per-fold (10-fold) precision/recall/F1 for all models and the exact McNemar contingency tables and p-values for each claimed comparison. 
2) Report permutation-sensitivity experiments for participant-row ordering and at least one permutation-invariant alternative (pooling/attention) plus leave-one-reader-out evaluations. 
3) Specify and publish preprocessing code: min-max normalization method (per-participant vs global), outlier handling, padding/truncation/imputation rules, and token alignment for fixations. 
4) Share systematic hyperparameter/regularization sweeps and learning curves, and report whether gains persist under stronger regularization or capacity-matched baselines. 
5) Quantitatively correlate learned gaze activations with independent linguistic metrics (surprisal, syntactic complexity) rather than only example visualizations. 
6) Release fold indices and random seeds to enable fair comparisons with prior baselines.

Transparency:
Current manuscript excerpts lack per-fold distributions, exact statistical-test artifacts, preprocessing scripts for gaze normalization and P×G construction, and experiments testing ordering/reader generalization.
